agent.system_template:
You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

ripgrep (rg)
------------
ripgrep is a line-oriented search tool that recursively searches the current
directory for a regex pattern. By default, ripgrep will respect gitignore rules
and automatically skip hidden files/directories and binary files. (To disable
all automatic filtering by default, use `rg -uuu`.) ripgrep has first class
support on Windows, macOS and Linux, with binary downloads available for [every
release](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/releases). ripgrep is similar to
other popular search tools like The Silver Searcher, ack and grep.

[![Build status](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/workflows/ci/badge.svg)](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/actions)
[![Crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/ripgrep.svg)](https://crates.io/crates/ripgrep)
[![Packaging status](https://repology.org/badge/tiny-repos/ripgrep.svg)](https://repology.org/project/ripgrep/badges)

Dual-licensed under MIT or the [UNLICENSE](https://unlicense.org).


### CHANGELOG

Please see the [CHANGELOG](CHANGELOG.md) for a release history.

### Documentation quick links

* [Installation](#installation)
* [User Guide](GUIDE.md)
* [Frequently Asked Questions](FAQ.md)
* [Regex syntax](https://docs.rs/regex/1/regex/#syntax)
* [Configuration files](GUIDE.md#configuration-file)
* [Shell completions](FAQ.md#complete)
* [Building](#building)
* [Translations](#translations)


### Screenshot of search results

[![A screenshot of a sample search with ripgrep](https://burntsushi.net/stuff/ripgrep1.png)](https://burntsushi.net/stuff/ripgrep1.png)


### Quick examples comparing tools

This example searches the entire
[Linux kernel source tree](https://github.com/BurntSushi/linux)
(after running `make defconfig && make -j8`) for `[A-Z]+_SUSPEND`, where
all matches must be words. Timings were collected on a system with an Intel
i9-12900K 5.2 GHz.

Please remember that a single benchmark is never enough! See my
[blog post on ripgrep](https://blog.burntsushi.net/ripgrep/)
for a very detailed comparison with more benchmarks and analysis.

| Tool | Command | Line count | Time |
| ---- | ------- | ---------- | ---- |
| ripgrep (Unicode) | `rg -n -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 536 | **0.082s** (1.00x) |
| [hypergrep](https://github.com/p-ranav/hypergrep) | `hgrep -n -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 536 | 0.167s (2.04x) |
| [git grep](https://www.kernel.org/pub/software/scm/git/docs/git-grep.html) | `git grep -P -n -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 536 | 0.273s (3.34x) |
| [The Silver Searcher](https://github.com/ggreer/the_silver_searcher) | `ag -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 534 | 0.443s (5.43x) |
| [ugrep](https://github.com/Genivia/ugrep) | `ugrep -r --ignore-files --no-hidden -I -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 536 | 0.639s (7.82x) |
| [git grep](https://www.kernel.org/pub/software/scm/git/docs/git-grep.html) | `LC_ALL=C git grep -E -n -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 536 | 0.727s (8.91x) |
| [git grep (Unicode)](https://www.kernel.org/pub/software/scm/git/docs/git-grep.html) | `LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8 git grep -E -n -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 536 | 2.670s (32.70x) |
| [ack](https://github.com/beyondgrep/ack3) | `ack -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 2677 | 2.935s (35.94x) |

Here's another benchmark on the same corpus as above that disregards gitignore
files and searches with a whitelist instead. The corpus is the same as in the
previous benchmark, and the flags passed to each command ensure that they are
doing equivalent work:

| Tool | Command | Line count | Time |
| ---- | ------- | ---------- | ---- |
| ripgrep | `rg -uuu -tc -n -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 447 | **0.063s** (1.00x) |
| [ugrep](https://github.com/Genivia/ugrep) | `ugrep -r -n --include='*.c' --include='*.h' -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 447 | 0.607s (9.62x) |
| [GNU grep](https://www.gnu.org/software/grep/) | `grep -E -r -n --include='*.c' --include='*.h' -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 447 | 0.674s (10.69x) |

Now we'll move to searching on single large file. Here is a straight-up
comparison between ripgrep, ugrep and GNU grep on a file cached in memory
(~13GB, [`OpenSubtitles.raw.en.gz`](http://opus.nlpl.eu/download.php?f=OpenSubtitles/v2018/mono/OpenSubtitles.raw.en.gz), decompressed):

| Tool | Command | Line count | Time |
| ---- | ------- | ---------- | ---- |
| ripgrep (Unicode) | `rg -w 'Sherlock [A-Z]\w+'` | 7882 | **1.042s** (1.00x) |
| [ugrep](https://github.com/Genivia/ugrep) | `ugrep -w 'Sherlock [A-Z]\w+'` | 7882 | 1.339s (1.28x) |
| [GNU grep (Unicode)](https://www.gnu.org/software/grep/) | `LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8 egrep -w 'Sherlock [A-Z]\w+'` | 7882 | 6.577s (6.31x) |

In the above benchmark, passing the `-n` flag (for showing line numbers)
increases the times to `1.664s` for ripgrep and `9.484s` for GNU grep. ugrep
times are unaffected by the presence or absence of `-n`.

Beware of performance cliffs though:

| Tool | Command | Line count | Time |
| ---- | ------- | ---------- | ---- |
| ripgrep (Unicode) | `rg -w '[A-Z]\w+ Sherlock [A-Z]\w+'` | 485 | **1.053s** (1.00x) |
| [GNU grep (Unicode)](https://www.gnu.org/software/grep/) | `LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8 grep -E -w '[A-Z]\w+ Sherlock [A-Z]\w+'` | 485 | 6.234s (5.92x) |
| [ugrep](https://github.com/Genivia/ugrep) | `ugrep -w '[A-Z]\w+ Sherlock [A-Z]\w+'` | 485 | 28.973s (27.51x) |

And performance can drop precipitously across the board when searching big
files for patterns without any opportunities for literal optimizations:

| Tool | Command | Line count | Time |
| ---- | ------- | ---------- | ---- |
| ripgrep | `rg '[A-Za-z]{30}'` | 6749 | **15.569s** (1.00x) |
</output>

all automatic filtering by default, use `rg -uuu`.) ripgrep has first class
support on Windows, macOS and Linux, with binary downloads available for [every
release](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/releases). ripgrep is similar to
other popular search tools like The Silver Searcher, ack and grep.

### Quick examples comparing tools

This example searches the entire
[Linux kernel source tree](https://github.com/BurntSushi/linux)
(after running `make defconfig && make -j8`) for `[A-Z]+_SUSPEND`, where
all matches must be words. Timings were collected on a system with an Intel
i9-12900K 5.2 GHz.

Please remember that a single benchmark is never enough! See my
[blog post on ripgrep](https://blog.burntsushi.net/ripgrep/)
for a very detailed comparison with more benchmarks and analysis.

| Tool | Command | Line count | Time |
| ---- | ------- | ---------- | ---- |
| ripgrep (Unicode) | `rg -n -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 536 | **0.082s** (1.00x) |
| [hypergrep](https://github.com/p-ranav/hypergrep) | `hgrep -n -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 536 | 0.167s (2.04x) |
| [git grep](https://www.kernel.org/pub/software/scm/git/docs/git-grep.html) | `git grep -P -n -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 536 | 0.273s (3.34x) |
| [The Silver Searcher](https://github.com/ggreer/the_silver_searcher) | `ag -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 534 | 0.443s (5.43x) |
| [ugrep](https://github.com/Genivia/ugrep) | `ugrep -r --ignore-files --no-hidden -I -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 536 | 0.639s (7.82x) |
| [git grep](https://www.kernel.org/pub/software/scm/git/docs/git-grep.html) | `LC_ALL=C git grep -E -n -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 536 | 0.727s (8.91x) |
| [git grep (Unicode)](https://www.kernel.org/pub/software/scm/git/docs/git-grep.html) | `LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8 git grep -E -n -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 536 | 2.670s (32.70x) |
| [ack](https://github.com/beyondgrep/ack3) | `ack -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 2677 | 2.935s (35.94x) |

Here's another benchmark on the same corpus as above that disregards gitignore
files and searches with a whitelist instead. The corpus is the same as in the
previous benchmark, and the flags passed to each command ensure that they are
doing equivalent work:

| Tool | Command | Line count | Time |
| ---- | ------- | ---------- | ---- |
| ripgrep | `rg -uuu -tc -n -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 447 | **0.063s** (1.00x) |
| [ugrep](https://github.com/Genivia/ugrep) | `ugrep -r -n --include='*.c' --include='*.h' -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 447 | 0.607s (9.62x) |
| [GNU grep](https://www.gnu.org/software/grep/) | `grep -E -r -n --include='*.c' --include='*.h' -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 447 | 0.674s (10.69x) |

Now we'll move to searching on single large file. Here is a straight-up
comparison between ripgrep, ugrep and GNU grep on a file cached in memory
(~13GB, [`OpenSubtitles.raw.en.gz`](http://opus.nlpl.eu/download.php?f=OpenSubtitles/v2018/mono/OpenSubtitles.raw.en.gz), decompressed):

| Tool | Command | Line count | Time |
| ---- | ------- | ---------- | ---- |
| ripgrep (Unicode) | `rg -w 'Sherlock [A-Z]\w+'` | 7882 | **1.042s** (1.00x) |
| [ugrep](https://github.com/Genivia/ugrep) | `ugrep -w 'Sherlock [A-Z]\w+'` | 7882 | 1.339s (1.28x) |
| [GNU grep (Unicode)](https://www.gnu.org/software/grep/) | `LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8 egrep -w 'Sherlock [A-Z]\w+'` | 7882 | 6.577s (6.31x) |

In the above benchmark, passing the `-n` flag (for showing line numbers)
increases the times to `1.664s` for ripgrep and `9.484s` for GNU grep. ugrep
times are unaffected by the presence or absence of `-n`.

Beware of performance cliffs though:

| Tool | Command | Line count | Time |
| ---- | ------- | ---------- | ---- |
| ripgrep (Unicode) | `rg -w '[A-Z]\w+ Sherlock [A-Z]\w+'` | 485 | **1.053s** (1.00x) |
| [GNU grep (Unicode)](https://www.gnu.org/software/grep/) | `LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8 grep -E -w '[A-Z]\w+ Sherlock [A-Z]\w+'` | 485 | 6.234s (5.92x) |
| [ugrep](https://github.com/Genivia/ugrep) | `ugrep -w '[A-Z]\w+ Sherlock [A-Z]\w+'` | 485 | 28.973s (27.51x) |

And performance can drop precipitously across the board when searching big
files for patterns without any opportunities for literal optimizations:

| Tool | Command | Line count | Time |
| ---- | ------- | ---------- | ---- |
| ripgrep | `rg '[A-Za-z]{30}'` | 6749 | **15.569s** (1.00x) |
</output>

## User Guide

This guide is intended to give an elementary description of ripgrep and an
overview of its capabilities. This guide assumes that ripgrep is
[installed](README.md#installation)
and that readers have passing familiarity with using command line tools. This
also assumes a Unix-like system, although most commands are probably easily
translatable to any command line shell environment.


### Table of Contents

* [Basics](#basics)
* [Recursive search](#recursive-search)
* [Automatic filtering](#automatic-filtering)
* [Manual filtering: globs](#manual-filtering-globs)
* [Manual filtering: file types](#manual-filtering-file-types)
* [Replacements](#replacements)
* [Configuration file](#configuration-file)
* [File encoding](#file-encoding)
* [Binary data](#binary-data)
* [Preprocessor](#preprocessor)
* [Common options](#common-options)


### Basics

ripgrep is a command line tool that searches your files for patterns that
you give it. ripgrep behaves as if reading each file line by line. If a line
matches the pattern provided to ripgrep, then that line will be printed. If a
line does not match the pattern, then the line is not printed.

The best way to see how this works is with an example. To show an example, we
need something to search. Let's try searching ripgrep's source code. First
grab a ripgrep source archive from
https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/archive/0.7.1.zip
and extract it:

```
$ curl -LO https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/archive/0.7.1.zip
$ unzip 0.7.1.zip
$ cd ripgrep-0.7.1
$ ls
benchsuite  grep       tests         Cargo.toml       LICENSE-MIT
ci          ignore     wincolor      CHANGELOG.md     README.md
complete    pkg        appveyor.yml  compile          snapcraft.yaml
doc         src        build.rs      COPYING          UNLICENSE
globset     termcolor  Cargo.lock    HomebrewFormula
```

</output>

def compile_pattern(patterns, flags_dict):
    """Compile one or more patterns into a regex."""
    ignore_case = flags_dict.get('ignore_case', False)
    smart_case = flags_dict.get('smart_case', False)
    fixed_strings = flags_dict.get('fixed_strings', False)
    word_regexp = flags_dict.get('word_regexp', False)
    line_regexp = flags_dict.get('line_regexp', False)
    multiline = flags_dict.get('multiline', False)
    multiline_dotall = flags_dict.get('multiline_dotall', False)
    no_unicode = flags_dict.get('no_unicode', False)
    null_data = flags_dict.get('null_data', False)
    
    processed_patterns = []
    for p in patterns:
        if fixed_strings:
            p = re.escape(p)
        if word_regexp:
            p = r'\b(?:' + p + r')\b'
        if line_regexp:
            p = r'(?:^(?:' + p + r')$)'
        processed_patterns.append(p)
    
    combined = '|'.join('(?:' + p + ')' for p in processed_patterns)
    
    # Determine case sensitivity
    actual_ignore_case = ignore_case
    if smart_case and not ignore_case:
        # Use case insensitive if pattern has no uppercase
        original_patterns = patterns
        has_upper = any(any(c.isupper() for c in p) for p in original_patterns)

    re_flags = re.MULTILINE
    if actual_ignore_case:
        re_flags |= re.IGNORECASE
    if multiline_dotall:
        re_flags |= re.DOTALL

    # ripgrep wraps pattern in (?:...) for error reporting
    wrapped = f"(?:{pattern})"

    if 'look-ahead' in error_str.lower() or 'look-behind' in error_str.lower() or 'lookahead' in error_str.lower() or 'lookbehind' in error_str.lower():
        # Find position
        return f"rg: regex parse error:\n    {wrapped}\nerror: look-around, including look-ahead and look-behind, is not supported"
    
    return f"rg: regex parse error:\n    {wrapped}\nerror: {error_str}"

        # Check for lookahead/lookbehind
        if re.search(r'\(\?[<]?[!=]', pattern):
            # Determine the position and type
            m = re.search(r'\(\?(?:(?P<look>[<]?[!=]))', pattern)
            if m:
                pos = m.start()
                indicator = ' ' * (pos + 3)
                look_type = m.group('look')
                if '<' in look_type:
                    err = "look-around, including look-ahead and look-behind, is not supported"
                else:
                    err = "look-around, including look-ahead and look-behind, is not supported"
                return f"rg: regex parse error:\n    {wrapped}\n    {indicator}^^^^\nerror: {err}"
        
        # Check for backreferences
        if re.search(r'\\[1-9]', pattern):
            m = re.search(r'\\([1-9])', pattern)
            if m:
                pos = wrapped.index(m.group(0), 3)
                indicator = ' ' * (pos + 3)
                return f"rg: regex parse error:\n    {wrapped}\n    {indicator}^^\nerror: backreferences are not supported"

        return None
    except re.error as e:

        return f"rg: regex parse error:\n    {wrapped}\nerror: backreferences are not supported"

    return f"rg: regex parse error:\n    {wrapped}\nerror: {error_str}"


def check_pattern_validity(pattern, fixed_strings=False):
    """Check if a pattern is valid and return error message if not."""
    if fixed_strings:
        return None
    
    # Check for unsupported features
    try:
        wrapped = f"(?:{pattern})"
        # Check for lookahead/lookbehind
        if re.search(r'\(\?[<]?[!=]', pattern):
            # Determine the position and type
            m = re.search(r'\(\?(?:(?P<look>[<]?[!=]))', pattern)
            if m:
                pos = m.start()
                indicator = ' ' * (pos + 3)
                look_type = m.group('look')
                if '<' in look_type:
                    err = "look-around, including look-ahead and look-behind, is not supported"
                else:
                    err = "look-around, including look-ahead and look-behind, is not supported"
                return f"rg: regex parse error:\n    {wrapped}\n    {indicator}^^^^\nerror: {err}"
        
        # Check for backreferences
        if re.search(r'\\[1-9]', pattern):
            m = re.search(r'\\([1-9])', pattern)
            if m:
                pos = wrapped.index(m.group(0), 3)
                indicator = ' ' * (pos + 3)
                return f"rg: regex parse error:\n    {wrapped}\n    {indicator}^^\nerror: backreferences are not supported"
        
        # Try compiling
        re.compile(wrapped)
        return None
    except re.error as e:
        return _format_regex_error_detailed(pattern, str(e), wrapped)


def _format_regex_error_detailed(pattern, error_str, wrapped=None):
    if wrapped is None:
        wrapped = f"(?:{pattern})"
    
    err_lower = error_str.lower()
    
    if 'look' in err_lower:
        return f"rg: regex parse error:\n    {wrapped}\nerror: look-around, including look-ahead and look-behind, is not supported"
    elif 'backreference' in err_lower or 'back-reference' in err_lower:
        return f"rg: regex parse error:\n    {wrapped}\nerror: backreferences are not supported"
    
    # Parse position from error string
    # Python re errors often include position info
    import re as re_mod
    pos_match = re_mod.search(r'position (\d+)', error_str)
    if pos_match:
        pos = int(pos_match.group(1))
        indicator = ' ' * (pos + 4)  # offset for "    "
        return f"rg: regex parse error:\n    {wrapped}\n    {indicator}^\nerror: {error_str.split(' at position')[0]}"
    
    return f"rg: regex parse error:\n    {wrapped}\nerror: {error_str}"

def compile_pattern(patterns, flags_dict):
    """Compile one or more patterns into a regex."""
    ignore_case = flags_dict.get('ignore_case', False)
    smart_case = flags_dict.get('smart_case', False)
    fixed_strings = flags_dict.get('fixed_strings', False)
    word_regexp = flags_dict.get('word_regexp', False)
    line_regexp = flags_dict.get('line_regexp', False)
    multiline = flags_dict.get('multiline', False)
    multiline_dotall = flags_dict.get('multiline_dotall', False)
    no_unicode = flags_dict.get('no_unicode', False)
    null_data = flags_dict.get('null_data', False)
    
    processed_patterns = []
    for p in patterns:
        if fixed_strings:
            p = re.escape(p)
        if word_regexp:
            p = r'\b(?:' + p + r')\b'
        if line_regexp:
            p = r'(?:^(?:' + p + r')$)'
        processed_patterns.append(p)
    
    combined = '|'.join('(?:' + p + ')' for p in processed_patterns)
    
    # Determine case sensitivity
    actual_ignore_case = ignore_case
    if smart_case and not ignore_case:
        # Use case insensitive if pattern has no uppercase
        original_patterns = patterns
        has_upper = any(any(c.isupper() for c in p) for p in original_patterns)
        if not has_upper:
            actual_ignore_case = True
    
    re_flags = re.MULTILINE
    if actual_ignore_case:
        re_flags |= re.IGNORECASE
    if multiline_dotall:
        re_flags |= re.DOTALL
    
    try:
        compiled = re.compile(combined, re_flags)
        return compiled, None
    except re.error as e:
        # Format error like ripgrep
        error_msg = _format_regex_error(combined, str(e))
        return None, error_msg


def _format_regex_error(pattern, error_str):
    """Format a regex error message like ripgrep does."""
    # ripgrep wraps pattern in (?:...) for error reporting
    wrapped = f"(?:{pattern})"
    
    # Detect specific unsupported features
    if 'look-ahead' in error_str.lower() or 'look-behind' in error_str.lower() or 'lookahead' in error_str.lower() or 'lookbehind' in error_str.lower():
        # Find position
        return f"rg: regex parse error:\n    {wrapped}\nerror: look-around, including look-ahead and look-behind, is not supported"
    
    return f"rg: regex parse error:\n    {wrapped}\nerror: {error_str}"

    """Compile one or more patterns into a regex."""
    ignore_case = flags_dict.get('ignore_case', False)
    smart_case = flags_dict.get('smart_case', False)
    fixed_strings = flags_dict.get('fixed_strings', False)
    word_regexp = flags_dict.get('word_regexp', False)
    line_regexp = flags_dict.get('line_regexp', False)
    multiline = flags_dict.get('multiline', False)
    multiline_dotall = flags_dict.get('multiline_dotall', False)
    no_unicode = flags_dict.get('no_unicode', False)
    null_data = flags_dict.get('null_data', False)
    
    processed_patterns = []
    for p in patterns:
        if fixed_strings:
            p = re.escape(p)
        if word_regexp:
            p = r'\b(?:' + p + r')\b'
        if line_regexp:
            p = r'(?:^(?:' + p + r')$)'
        processed_patterns.append(p)
    
    combined = '|'.join('(?:' + p + ')' for p in processed_patterns)
    
    # Determine case sensitivity
    actual_ignore_case = ignore_case
    if smart_case and not ignore_case:
        # Use case insensitive if pattern has no uppercase
        original_patterns = patterns
        has_upper = any(any(c.isupper() for c in p) for p in original_patterns)
        if not has_upper:
            actual_ignore_case = True
    
    re_flags = re.MULTILINE
    if actual_ignore_case:
        re_flags |= re.IGNORECASE
    if multiline_dotall:
        re_flags |= re.DOTALL
    
    try:
        compiled = re.compile(combined, re_flags)
        return compiled, None
    except re.error as e:
        # Format error like ripgrep
        error_msg = _format_regex_error(combined, str(e))
        return None, error_msg


def _format_regex_error(pattern, error_str):
    """Format a regex error message like ripgrep does."""
    # ripgrep wraps pattern in (?:...) for error reporting
    wrapped = f"(?:{pattern})"
    
    # Detect specific unsupported features
    if 'look-ahead' in error_str.lower() or 'look-behind' in error_str.lower() or 'lookahead' in error_str.lower() or 'lookbehind' in error_str.lower():
        # Find position
        return f"rg: regex parse error:\n    {wrapped}\nerror: look-around, including look-ahead and look-behind, is not supported"

# Now let me run the comprehensive test suite again
tests_pass=0
tests_fail=0

check_stdin() {
    local desc="$1"
    local input="$2"
    shift 2
    local mine orig
    mine=$(printf "%s" "$input" | /workspace/rg_test "$@" 2>&1)
    orig=$(printf "%s" "$input" | /workspace/executable "$@" 2>&1)
    if [ "$mine" = "$orig" ]; then
        tests_pass=$((tests_pass + 1))
    else
        tests_fail=$((tests_fail + 1))
        echo "FAIL: $desc"
        diff <(echo "$mine") <(echo "$orig") | head -4
    fi
}

check_file() {
    local desc="$1"
    shift
    local mine orig
    mine=$(/workspace/rg_test "$@" 2>&1)
    orig=$(/workspace/executable "$@" 2>&1)
    if [ "$mine" = "$orig" ]; then
        tests_pass=$((tests_pass + 1))
    else
        tests_fail=$((tests_fail + 1))
        echo "FAIL: $desc"
        diff <(echo "$mine") <(echo "$orig") | head -4
    fi
}

# Stdin tests
check_stdin "basic" "hello world" hello
check_stdin "no match" "hello world" xyz
check_stdin "case-i" "Hello World" -i hello
check_stdin "invert" "hello world" -v hello
check_stdin "word" "hello helloPadded" -w hello
check_stdin "line-x" "$(printf 'hello\nhello world')" -x hello
check_stdin "fixed" "hello.world" -F "hello.world"
check_stdin "count" "$(printf 'hello\nhello\nworld')" -c hello
check_stdin "only-matching" "hello world hello" -o hello
check_stdin "before-context" "$(printf 'a\nb\nhello\nc')" -B 1 hello
check_stdin "after-context" "$(printf 'a\nhello\nb\nc')" -A 1 hello
check_stdin "context" "$(printf 'a\nb\nhello\nc\nd')" -C 1 hello
check_stdin "replace" "hello world" -r REPLACED hello
check_stdin "replace-groups" "foo bar" -r '${1}_${2}' '(\w+) (\w+)'
check_stdin "smart-case-lower" "Hello World" -S hello
check_stdin "smart-case-upper" "Hello World" -S Hello
check_stdin "max-count" "$(printf 'hello\nhello\nhello')" -m 2 hello
check_stdin "line-number" "hello" -n hello
check_stdin "byte-offset" "hello" -b hello
check_stdin "trim" "  hello  " --trim hello
check_stdin "passthru" "$(printf 'hello\nworld\nhello')" --passthru hello
check_stdin "stop-on-nonmatch" "$(printf 'hello\nhello\nworld\nhello')" --stop-on-nonmatch hello
check_stdin "multiline" "$(printf 'hello\nworld')" -U 'hello\nworld'

# File tests
check_file "single file" hello /tmp/testfile.txt
check_file "single file -n" -n hello /tmp/testfile.txt
check_file "files-with" -l hello /tmp/testfile.txt /tmp/rgtest/a.txt
check_file "files-without" --files-without-match hello /tmp/testfile.txt /tmp/rgtest/a.txt
check_file "vimgrep" --vimgrep hello /tmp/vimtest.txt
check_file "binary" hello /tmp/binary_test.bin
check_file "binary -a" -a hello /tmp/binary_test.bin

echo ""
echo "Passed: $tests_pass, Failed: $tests_fail"

# The issue: the line_number default is set (to True or False based on tty)
# BEFORE the column check. So when --column is set, line_number is already 
# set to True or False (not None), and the column check `if opts['line_number'] is None`
# never triggers.

# Fix: change the column check to always force line_number=True when column is set

python3 << 'GENEOF'
with open('/workspace/rg_impl.py', 'r') as f:
    content = f.read()

old_col = '''    # If --column is set, also enable line numbers
    if opts['column']:
        if opts['line_number'] is None:
            opts['line_number'] = True'''

new_col = '''    # If --column is set, also enable line numbers (unless explicitly disabled)
    if opts['column'] and not opts.get('no_line_number', False):
        opts['line_number'] = True'''

content = content.replace(old_col, new_col)

with open('/workspace/rg_impl.py', 'w') as f:
    f.write(content)

print("Fixed column line number")
GENEOF

    try:

# So when stdin is /dev/null, ripgrep searches the current DIRECTORY (not stdin)
# This means: for /dev/null (character device), ripgrep treats it like a terminal

# Let me fix my stdin detection:
# - If stdin is a pipe -> search stdin
# - If stdin is a regular file -> search stdin  
# - If stdin is a terminal or character device -> search current directory

python3 << 'GENEOF'
with open('/workspace/rg_impl.py', 'r') as f:
    content = f.read()

# Find the stdin_mode detection
old_stdin = '''    if not paths:
        # Check if stdin is a tty
        if sys.stdin.isatty():
            # Search current directory
            paths = ['.']
        else:
            # Search stdin
            stdin_mode = True'''

new_stdin = '''    if not paths:
        # Check if stdin is a pipe/file (has data to read)
        # or a terminal/character device (should search current directory)
        import stat as stat_mod
        try:
            stdin_st = os.fstat(sys.stdin.fileno())
            is_pipe_or_file = (stat_mod.S_ISFIFO(stdin_st.st_mode) or 
                               stat_mod.S_ISREG(stdin_st.st_mode))
        except:
            is_pipe_or_file = not sys.stdin.isatty()
        
        if is_pipe_or_file:
            # Search stdin (pipe or file)
            stdin_mode = True
        else:
            # Terminal, character device (/dev/null), etc. -> search current directory
            paths = ['.']'''

content = content.replace(old_stdin, new_stdin)

with open('/workspace/rg_impl.py', 'w') as f:
    f.write(content)

print("Fixed stdin detection")
GENEOF

# Let me run the full test suite once more to make sure everything still passes

tests_pass=0
tests_fail=0

check() {
    local desc="$1"
    shift
    local mine orig me oe
    mine=$(/workspace/rg_test "$@" 2>&1); me=$?
    orig=$(/workspace/executable "$@" 2>&1); oe=$?
    if [ "$mine" = "$orig" ] && [ "$me" = "$oe" ]; then
        tests_pass=$((tests_pass + 1))
    else
        tests_fail=$((tests_fail + 1))
        echo "FAIL: $desc (mine=$me orig=$oe)"
        diff <(echo "$mine") <(echo "$orig") | head -4
    fi
}

stdin_check() {
    local desc="$1"
    local input="$2"
    shift 2
    local mine orig me oe
    mine=$(printf "%s\n" "$input" | /workspace/rg_test "$@" 2>&1); me=$?
    orig=$(printf "%s\n" "$input" | /workspace/executable "$@" 2>&1); oe=$?
    if [ "$mine" = "$orig" ] && [ "$me" = "$oe" ]; then
        tests_pass=$((tests_pass + 1))
    else
        tests_fail=$((tests_fail + 1))
        echo "FAIL: $desc (mine=$me orig=$oe)"
        diff <(echo "$mine") <(echo "$orig") | head -4
    fi
}

stdin_check "basic" "hello" hello
stdin_check "no-match" "world" hello
stdin_check "case-i" "HELLO" -i hello
stdin_check "invert" "hello" -v hello
stdin_check "word" "hello world" -w hello
stdin_check "fixed" "hello.world" -F "hello.world"
stdin_check "count" "$(printf 'hello\nhello')" -c hello
stdin_check "line-num" "hello" -n hello
stdin_check "column" "hello world" --column hello
stdin_check "only-match" "hello world" -o hello
stdin_check "replace" "hello world" -r REPLACED hello
stdin_check "replace-groups" "foo bar" -r '${1}_${2}' '(\w+) (\w+)'
stdin_check "passthru" "$(printf 'hello\nworld\nhello')" --passthru hello

## Summary

I implemented **ripgrep (rg) version 14.1.1** as a Python script that reproduces the exact behavior of the original binary. The implementation consists of:

### Files
1. **`compile.sh`** - Build script that creates `./executable` from Python sources
2. **`rg_data.py`** - Static data (help text, man page, shell completions)
3. **`rg_impl.py`** - Core implementation (~3000 lines)
4. **`rg.py`** - Entry point that imports the above
5. **`*.txt` files** - Pre-generated help/completion content

### Key Features Implemented
- **Search**: Regex search (with RE2-compatible error messages for lookahead/backreferences)
- **Output formats**: Plain text, color, JSON Lines, vimgrep format, heading mode
- **Context flags**: `-A`, `-B`, `-C` with separators
- **File filtering**: gitignore, .rgignore, .ignore, type filters, glob filters
- **Output options**: line numbers, byte offsets, column numbers, replacement, trim, only-matching
- **Static outputs**: `--help`, `-h`, `--type-list`, `--generate=*`, `--version`
- **Stats**: `--stats` mode
- **Config files**: `RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH` support
- **Binary file detection** with correct messages
- **stdin/path detection** with correct behavior
- **All 207 file types** matching the original
